blocks.text: Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms to citizens only, a point examiners repeat every year. The six freedoms are:

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
Key timeline points to memorise:
4. Article 19: the six freedoms and reasonable restrictions
blocks.text: - Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). - Freedom to assemble peaceably and without arms under Article 19(1)(b). - Freedom to form associations or unions under Article 19(1)(c). - Freedom to move freely throughout India under Article 19(1)(d). - Freedom to reside and settle in any part of India under Article 19(1)(e). - Freedom to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business under Article 19(1)(g). Note that the original clause (f) on property was removed by the Forty-fourth Amendment of 1978.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
Key timeline points to memorise:
4. Article 19: the six freedoms and reasonable restrictions
blocks.text: Each freedom is subject to reasonable restrictions in clauses (2) to (6), including the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, public order, decency, morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence. In 2015 the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act because vague limits on online speech were not reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
Key timeline points to memorise:
4. Article 19: the six freedoms and reasonable restrictions
blocks.text: Distinction: Article 19 protects the freedoms of citizens only, whereas Article 21 protects the life and liberty of all persons including non-citizens.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
Key timeline points to memorise:
5. Article 21: life, liberty and an expanding promise
blocks.text: Article 21 states that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. Before 1978 the phrase was read narrowly, but in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India in 1978 the Supreme Court held that the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable and not arbitrary or oppressive.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
Key timeline points to memorise:
5. Article 21: life, liberty and an expanding promise
blocks.text: Distinction: 'procedure established by law' as written in Article 21 means a procedure laid down by a validly enacted law, whereas 'due process of law' additionally demands that the law itself be fair and reasonable, and after Maneka Gandhi in 1978 the Court reads Article 21 as including due-process values.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
Key timeline points to memorise:
5. Article 21: life, liberty and an expanding promise
blocks.text: Since 1978 the Court has read many implied rights into Article 21, including the right to live with dignity, livelihood, shelter, health, a clean environment, speedy trial, legal aid, and, in 2017, privacy in the Puttaswamy judgment. Article 21A on education for children aged 6 to 14 years was inserted by the Eighty-sixth Amendment in 2002 and enforced through the 2009 education Act.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
Key timeline points to memorise:
5. Article 21: life, liberty and an expanding promise
blocks.text: Definition: 'Preventive detention' means detention of a person without trial on the apprehension that the person may commit a future offence, whereas punitive detention follows conviction for an offence already committed.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
Key timeline points to memorise:
6. Article 32: the right to Constitutional remedies
blocks.text: Article 32 gives every citizen the right to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the heart and soul of the Constitution. The Supreme Court has held that Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right, so Parliament cannot suspend it by an ordinary law.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
The Court issues five writs under Articles 32 and 226:
blocks.text: - Habeas corpus: to produce a detained person before the court. - Mandamus: to command a public authority to perform a legal duty. - Prohibition: to restrain a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction. - Certiorari: to quash the order of a lower court or tribunal. - Quo warranto: to question the authority by which a person holds a public office.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
The Court issues five writs under Articles 32 and 226:
blocks.text: Definition: A 'writ' is a written order issued by a constitutional court commanding a person or authority to do, or to refrain from doing, a specified act.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System

blocks.text: Distinction: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right and the Supreme Court must grant a remedy when a Fundamental Right is violated, whereas Article 226 is wider in scope but discretionary, covering Fundamental Rights and other legal rights before a High Court.

blocks.text: During the Emergency, the majority in ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla in 1976 held that Article 21 could be suspended; the Forty-fourth Amendment of 1978 then provided that Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during an Emergency.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
The Court issues five writs under Articles 32 and 226:
7. Physical geography of Assam and the Brahmaputra system
blocks.text: Assam lies in the eastern Himalayan foothills and the Brahmaputra valley. The state covers about 78,438 square kilometres, and the Brahmaputra valley is roughly 720 kilometres long from east to west and 80 to 100 kilometres wide. The Brahmaputra is a braided river across most of Assam, shifting channels, building sandbars called chars, and flooding heavily every monsoon.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
The Court issues five writs under Articles 32 and 226:
7. Physical geography of Assam and the Brahmaputra system
blocks.text: Definition: A 'braided river' is a wide, shallow river that splits into many interlacing channels around temporary sandbars and islands.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
The Court issues five writs under Articles 32 and 226:
7. Physical geography of Assam and the Brahmaputra system
blocks.text: Definition: 'Alluvium' is fertile silt, sand and clay deposited by rivers, and the Brahmaputra valley floor is almost entirely recent alluvium.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
The Court issues five writs under Articles 32 and 226:
7. Physical geography of Assam and the Brahmaputra system
blocks.text: The Brahmaputra rises as the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet near the Chemayungdung glacier, flows about 2,900 kilometres in total, enters Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang or Dihang, becomes the Brahmaputra in Assam after joining the Dibang and Lohit at Kobo, and leaves Assam at Dhubri to enter Bangladesh as the Jamuna. Within Assam the river flows for about 640 kilometres. Majuli, formed between the Brahmaputra and the Subansiri-Luit channels, is among the largest inhabited river islands in the world, though erosion has shrunk it from over 1,200 square kilometres a century ago to roughly 350 to 500 square kilometres today.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System
The Court issues five writs under Articles 32 and 226:
7. Physical geography of Assam and the Brahmaputra system
blocks.text: The earthquake of 15 August 1950, measuring 8.6 in magnitude, tilted tributary gradients, raised the river bed in places, and intensified floods and bank erosion across Upper Assam. The Brahmaputra Board was set up in 1982 under the Brahmaputra Board Act of 1981 to plan flood control in the valley.

blocks.text: Assam has three broad soil zones: recent alluvial soils of the flood plains, old alluvial soils of the higher terraces, and laterite and red soils on the Karbi and Dima Hasao hills with patches of forest soil.

section_path: Exam Study Notes: Fundamental Rights and the Brahmaputra System

9. Soils, climate and key numbers of Assam
blocks.text: The climate is humid subtropical with a strong monsoon. Average annual rainfall for the state is about 2,300 millimetres, with Cherrapunji-Mawsynram just across the border in Meghalaya receiving over 11,000 millimetres in extreme years. Summer temperatures range from 30 to 35 degrees Celsius in the valley, winter minimums fall to 6 to 10 degrees Celsius, and relative humidity stays between 70 and 85 percent for much of the year. Roughly 75 percent of annual rain falls between June and September, and the state records floods in most years: the devastating floods of 2022 affected all 35 districts and over 5.8 million people, while the 2011 census recorded Assam at about 31.2 million people with a density near 398 persons per square kilometre.

How to use these notes

These notes combine two high-yield exam areas: Indian Polity (Fundamental Rights, Articles 12 to 35) and the Physical Geography of Assam with the Brahmaputra river system. Read each section, memorise the definitions, learn the distinctions, and test yourself with the tables and numbers at the end of each section.

1. Fundamental Rights: Articles 12 to 35, an overview

The Constitution of India was adopted on 26 November 1949 and the Fundamental Rights in Part III entered into force on 26 January 1950. Fundamental Rights are contained in Articles 12 to 35 of the Constitution. They are justiciable, which means a citizen can move the Supreme Court under Article 32 or a High Court under Article 226 when a right is violated.

Definition: The term 'State' under Article 12 includes the Government and Parliament of India, the Government and legislature of each State, all local authorities, and all other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.

Definition: 'Law' under Article 13 includes any ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law in the territory of India.

Article 13 declares that all laws in force before 26 January 1950 that are inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void to the extent of the inconsistency. It also bars the State from making any law that takes away or abridges the rights conferred by Part III. The First Amendment of 1951 added clause (4) to Article 13 protection for land-reform laws and inserted Articles 31A and 31B with the Ninth Schedule. The Forty-second Amendment of 1976 attempted to shield all Directive Principles from Articles 14 and 19, but the Forty-fourth Amendment of 1978 rolled back the worst excesses of the Emergency and deleted the right to property as a Fundamental Right.

Key timeline points to memorise:

Union of India. - 2017: the nine-judge bench in Justice K. S. Puttaswamy v. 3. Article 14 and the equality code of Articles 15 and 16

Definition: 'Equality before the law' means the absence of any special privilege for any person, while 'equal protection of the laws' means equals must be treated equally and a reasonable classification of persons is permitted.

Distinction: equality before the law is a negative concept that denies special privilege, whereas equal protection of the laws is a positive concept that permits reasonable classification of equals and unequals.

Article 15 applies to both the State and, in some clauses, private individuals running public places such as shops, wells, roads and places of public resort. Article 16 applies to employment under the State. Article 15(3) permits special provisions for women and children, Article 15(4) added in 1951 permits special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, and Articles 15(5) and 15(6) extend reservations to private educational institutions and to Economically Weaker Sections respectively. Article 16(4) permits reservation in favour of backward classes, Article 16(4A) permits reservation in promotion for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and Article 16(6) inserted in 2019 permits up to 10 percent reservation for Economically Weaker Sections.

4. Article 19: the six freedoms and reasonable restrictions

Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms to citizens only, a point examiners repeat every year. The six freedoms are:

- Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). - Freedom to assemble peaceably and without arms under Article 19(1)(b). - Freedom to form associations or unions under Article 19(1)(c). - Freedom to move freely throughout India under Article 19(1)(d). - Freedom to reside and settle in any part of India under Article 19(1)(e). - Freedom to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business under Article 19(1)(g). Note that the original clause (f) on property was removed by the Forty-fourth Amendment of 1978.

Each freedom is subject to reasonable restrictions in clauses (2) to (6), including the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, public order, decency, morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence. In 2015 the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act because vague limits on online speech were not reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).

Distinction: Article 19 protects the freedoms of citizens only, whereas Article 21 protects the life and liberty of all persons including non-citizens.

5. Article 21: life, liberty and an expanding promise

Article 21 states that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. Before 1978 the phrase was read narrowly, but in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India in 1978 the Supreme Court held that the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable and not arbitrary or oppressive.

Distinction: 'procedure established by law' as written in Article 21 means a procedure laid down by a validly enacted law, whereas 'due process of law' additionally demands that the law itself be fair and reasonable, and after Maneka Gandhi in 1978 the Court reads Article 21 as including due-process values.

Since 1978 the Court has read many implied rights into Article 21, including the right to live with dignity, livelihood, shelter, health, a clean environment, speedy trial, legal aid, and, in 2017, privacy in the Puttaswamy judgment. Article 21A on education for children aged 6 to 14 years was inserted by the Eighty-sixth Amendment in 2002 and enforced through the 2009 education Act.

Definition: 'Preventive detention' means detention of a person without trial on the apprehension that the person may commit a future offence, whereas punitive detention follows conviction for an offence already committed.

6. Article 32: the right to Constitutional remedies

Article 32 gives every citizen the right to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the heart and soul of the Constitution. The Supreme Court has held that Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right, so Parliament cannot suspend it by an ordinary law.

The Court issues five writs under Articles 32 and 226:

- Habeas corpus: to produce a detained person before the court. - Mandamus: to command a public authority to perform a legal duty. - Prohibition: to restrain a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction. - Certiorari: to quash the order of a lower court or tribunal. - Quo warranto: to question the authority by which a person holds a public office.

Definition: A 'writ' is a written order issued by a constitutional court commanding a person or authority to do, or to refrain from doing, a specified act.

Distinction: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right and the Supreme Court must grant a remedy when a Fundamental Right is violated, whereas Article 226 is wider in scope but discretionary, covering Fundamental Rights and other legal rights before a High Court.

During the Emergency, the majority in ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla in 1976 held that Article 21 could be suspended; the Forty-fourth Amendment of 1978 then provided that Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during an Emergency.

7. Physical geography of Assam and the Brahmaputra system

Assam lies in the eastern Himalayan foothills and the Brahmaputra valley. The state covers about 78,438 square kilometres, and the Brahmaputra valley is roughly 720 kilometres long from east to west and 80 to 100 kilometres wide. The Brahmaputra is a braided river across most of Assam, shifting channels, building sandbars called chars, and flooding heavily every monsoon.

Definition: A 'braided river' is a wide, shallow river that splits into many interlacing channels around temporary sandbars and islands.

Definition: 'Alluvium' is fertile silt, sand and clay deposited by rivers, and the Brahmaputra valley floor is almost entirely recent alluvium.

The Brahmaputra rises as the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet near the Chemayungdung glacier, flows about 2,900 kilometres in total, enters Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang or Dihang, becomes the Brahmaputra in Assam after joining the Dibang and Lohit at Kobo, and leaves Assam at Dhubri to enter Bangladesh as the Jamuna. Within Assam the river flows for about 640 kilometres. Majuli, formed between the Brahmaputra and the Subansiri-Luit channels, is among the largest inhabited river islands in the world, though erosion has shrunk it from over 1,200 square kilometres a century ago to roughly 350 to 500 square kilometres today.

The earthquake of 15 August 1950, measuring 8.6 in magnitude, tilted tributary gradients, raised the river bed in places, and intensified floods and bank erosion across Upper Assam. The Brahmaputra Board was set up in 1982 under the Brahmaputra Board Act of 1981 to plan flood control in the valley.

8. Tributaries of the Brahmaputra in Assam

Distinction: north-bank tributaries rise in the Himalayas, carry heavy silt, and build large alluvial fans, whereas south-bank tributaries rise in the hills of Meghalaya, Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh, carry less silt, and run in comparatively stable, narrower channels.

The principal tributaries examiners expect are:

North-bank tributaries:

- Subansiri: rises in Tibet, joins at Lakhimpur; about 442 kilometres long. - Ranganadi: rises in Arunachal Pradesh, joins near Lakhimpur. - Jia Bharali (Kameng): rises in Arunachal Pradesh, joins at Tezpur. - Puthimari: rises in Bhutan, joins near Kamrup. - Manas: rises in Bhutan, joins near Jogighopa; a major transboundary river about 376 kilometres long. - Sankosh (Gadadhar): forms part of the Assam-West Bengal boundary.

South-bank tributaries:

- Burhi Dihing: rises in the Patkai hills, joins near Dibrugarh. - Disang: rises in Nagaland, joins near Sibsagar. - Dikhow: rises in Nagaland, joins near Sibsagar. - Dhansiri: rises in Nagaland, joins near Golaghat; about 352 kilometres long. - Kopili: rises in Meghalaya, joins near Nagaon; about 256 kilometres long. - Kulsi and Krishnai: rise in Meghalaya and join in Lower Assam.

9. Soils, climate and key numbers of Assam

Assam has three broad soil zones: recent alluvial soils of the flood plains, old alluvial soils of the higher terraces, and laterite and red soils on the Karbi and Dima Hasao hills with patches of forest soil.

Distinction: khadar soils are newer, finer, low-lying alluvium renewed by almost every flood, whereas bhangar soils are older, coarser, higher-lying alluvium above the normal flood limit.

The climate is humid subtropical with a strong monsoon. Average annual rainfall for the state is about 2,300 millimetres, with Cherrapunji-Mawsynram just across the border in Meghalaya receiving over 11,000 millimetres in extreme years. Summer temperatures range from 30 to 35 degrees Celsius in the valley, winter minimums fall to 6 to 10 degrees Celsius, and relative humidity stays between 70 and 85 percent for much of the year. Roughly 75 percent of annual rain falls between June and September, and the state records floods in most years: the devastating floods of 2022 affected all 35 districts and over 5.8 million people, while the 2011 census recorded Assam at about 31.2 million people with a density near 398 persons per square kilometre.

Quick numbers for revision:

- Total length of the Brahmaputra: about 2,900 kilometres.

- Length inside Assam: about 640 kilometres.

- Valley length by 720 kilometres east-west; width 80 to 100 kilometres.

- State area: about 78,438 square kilometres.

- Average rainfall: about 2,300 millimetres per year.

- Majuli island today: roughly 350 to 500 square kilometres.

- 1950 earthquake magnitude: 8.6 on 15 August 1950.

- Brahmaputra Board set up in 1982.

- Floods of 2022: over 5.8 million people affected across 35 districts.

- 2011 census: Assam population about 31.2 million.
